summary: Alex Davies of WIRED argues that Smart's experiment of adapting a Forfour car to run on rails, the "Forrail," is a light-hearted PR stunt rather than a serious transit idea. The piece contends that the real benefits of personalized rapid transit (PRT) will come through self-driving cars rather than pods on tracks. It cites experts Sarah Kaufman and Paul Supawanich and notes that PRT systems have historically been costly and complicated, with many failures.
one_line: WIRED argues Smart's rail-running Forfour is a PR stunt, and that personalized rapid transit benefits will come via self-driving cars instead.
key_facts: Smart worked with train engineering outfit Interfleet to adapt a Forfour model for life on the rails, calling it "a light-hearted, one-off experiment."
The Forrail used 22-inch steel wheels weighing 176 pounds apiece in place of the car's wheels and tires.
The team disconnected the steering and welded aluminum supports between the axles to lock everything in position.
The Forrail ran along the privately operated Bluebell Railway in Sussex, England, during a model train show, covering 10 miles of track.
Smart said the experiment does "not encourage any individual to carry out similar modifications. It's incredibly difficult."
Sarah Kaufman is an adjunct assistant professor of planning at New York University.
The ULTra (Urban Light Transit) system at London Heathrow Airport has shuttled hundreds of thousands of passengers between one terminal and a parking lot since 2011.
Morgantown Personal Rapid Transit moves people between five West Virginia University campuses.
The Mineta Transportation Institute reported that PRT does not appear 'on the radar' of urban planners, transit professionals, or policy makers.
Paul Supawanich is a transportation planner at Remix, a startup that works with transit agencies.
Supawanich said putting a Smart car on tracks uses "very cost-intensive, heavy-duty infrastructure for a very low return."
The article says Smart is part of Daimler, which is working on autonomous technology for tractor trailers and Mercedes-Benz passenger cars.
Kaufman said: "There is a burgeoning movement towards personalized transit. And I think that will go hand in hand with automated vehicles."
Supawanich said self-driving cars could give the upsides of PRT and called it the "magical win-win," though they could enable sprawl.
The article concludes that autonomous cars will work much like a train, following one another and reducing congestion, with no steel wheels required.
